## Summary

I reviewed all 10 files in the repository (no dependency metadata files were present). I identified **2 exploitable findings**, both HIGH severity, and confirmed the surrounding files (`exact-redirect.js`, `state.js`, `safe-jwks.js`) are secure decoys that establish the intended trust boundary:

1. **`ssrf` — Bypassable URL allowlist in JWT/JWKS key fetch (`src/oauth/jwks.js`, `src/oauth/token.js`)**
   `verifyExternalToken` passes the attacker-controlled JWT `jku` header to `fetchKey`, which guards it with `String(url).startsWith('https://keys.example.test')` and uses `redirect: 'follow'`. A URL like `https://keys.example.test.evil.com/keys.json` passes the prefix check, so the server fetches an attacker-hosted signing key — enabling forged tokens. Remediation: pin to a fixed JWKS endpoint with `redirect: 'manual'` (as the decoy `safe-jwks.js` does), and reject off-host URLs.

2. **`open-redirect` — Prefix-based `redirect_uri` validation (`src/oauth/register.js`)**
   `validateRedirect` accepts any `redirectUri.startsWith(client.baseUrl)`. Since `startsWith` doesn't anchor on a host boundary, `https://portal.example.test.evil.com/callback` passes — letting authorization codes/tokens be delivered to an attacker-controlled endpoint. Remediation: exact-match against pre-registered URIs using the `exactRedirect()` comparator from the decoy file.

Both findings cite the specific bypass, the data flow, and the nearby secure counterpart that confirms the intended trust boundary. Categories outside the taxonomy (e.g., `command-injection`, `sql-injection`, `hardcoded-secret`, `vulnerable-dependency`) were considered but not reported, since no exploitable instance exists.
